catalog_quote: Klon has regular word stress. The vowel found in unstressed syllables is typically reduced to schwa. ... Stress may fall on either the ultimate or the penultimate syllable in disyllabic words, dependent on the status of the penultimate syllable. If the penultimate syllable is a heavy syllable, with the structure CV(V)C stress falls on it (e.g. ['boŋ.hɛp] ‘fog’). Otherwise, if the penultimate syllable is light, then the stress will fall on the ultimate syllable (e.g. [nə'mɛr] ‘wind’). ... There are very few underived words consisting of more than two syllables. There are two stress patterns found in trisyllabic words. ... In all trisyllabic words secondary stress falls on the ultimate syllable. However, they differ as to whether primary stress falls on the penultimate or pre-penultimate syllable. ... audit.reasoning: The coding (weight-sensitive: heavy CV(V)C penult else final in disyllables; heavier of antepenult/penult in trisyllables; initial in 4-syllable words) rests on the standard reference grammar, Baird 2008 (PL 596), ch.2 sec. 2.4 pp.22-23, which we hold; the deciding quotation and the sec. 1.8 summary line are verbatim in the held text at the stated locators. Glottolog lists no other grammar or phonology for Klon; the open-access family volume fetched sources now (Klamer ed. 2017) and Schapper 2020 (already held under kama1365) add no Klon-specific synchronic stress statement and confirm that AP stress is generally weight-attracted, consistent with the coding. One nuance worth keeping in the 'heavy' note: Baird p.22 says underived trisyllables have no codas in penult/antepenult, so 'heavier' there cannot be coda weight alone (examples suggest full vowel/VC vs schwa), which the record already flags

sources.citation: Klamer, Marian (ed.). 2017. The Alor-Pantar languages: History and typology. Second edition. (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 3.) Berlin: Language Science Press. Open access.
sources.quote: p.54: 'In most of the modern languages stress is on the penultimate syllable; however, stress may also be attracted to heavy syllables, as in Teiwa jiˈvar'. p.123: 'Klon /ə/ seems to originate in a short, unstressed pAP *a ... see Heston 2016 for a more complete stress-related account of Klon /ə/'. No synchronic Klon stress rule stated.
